messages.author: bafbff7f5abd72d1
messages.subject: Reporting question
parts:
As recommended, I fit two models:

```{r}
m1<-brm(CorrectedRt~Congruent+(1|Subject)+(1|Word), data = scta, family="gaussian", prior = prior, warmup = 2000, iter = 4000, chains = 20, save_all_pars = TRUE)
m0<-brm(CorrectedRt~(1|Subject)+(1|Word), data = scta, family="gaussian", prior = priornull, warmup = 2000, iter = 4000, chains = 20, save_all_pars = TRUE)
```

I.e., one with the parameter of interest, and one without.

I used the following priors:

```{r}
library(brms)
prior<-c(set_prior("cauchy(0, 2.5)",class = "b", coef = ""),set_prior("cauchy(0, 10)", class = "Intercept", coef = ""))
priornull<-c(set_prior("cauchy(0, 10)", class = "Intercept", coef = ""))
```

I run:
```{r}
bayes_factor(m0,m1)
```

I am interested in testing the null hypothesis that the parameter of interest (i.e., "Congruent") is equal to zero.

My question is whether this is an accurate report of what happened within brms?

We used the bayes_factor() command in the “brms” package to compare a model without and with the predictor of interest. This produces a value that approximates the probability that the data originate from a model in which the predictor of interest is equal to zero (i.e., the null hypothesis) vs. one in which it is free to vary (i.e., the alternate hypothesis).    

As a side note, the Bayes Factor was wildly large (i.e., 3.17e+42). Thus I also ran the analyses using two weakly informative priors recommended here, namely normal distributions with means of zero, and sds of either 1 or ten. Do you think this is adequate?

Thanks!

messages.author: 6e3dd74b422c061b
messages.subject: Re: [brms-users] Reporting question
parts:
I cannot tell whether these priors are reasonable, because I have no idea of the scale of your predictor.

Thus cauchy(0, 2.5) or normal(0, 1/10), may or may not be adequate. In particular the prior recommendation for the wiki you linked are for estimating and **not** for hypothesis testing with bayes factor. This is a completely different topic and setting priors for Bayes factors is hard.

I genrally recommend a sensitivity analysis in which you lets the scale of your priors vary across a reasonable scale and see how the Bayes factor changes.

The text you wrote appears reasonable to me thus far.

I have some more questions:

1) e+42 favoring which model?

2) What were the BFs with the normal priors?

3) Could you also show me the summary() output?

messages.subject: Re: [brms-users] Reporting question
parts:
Hey Paul

The predictor was dichotomous, and the outcome was continuous, ranging from about 300 to 3000 (reaction time in milliseconds). However, both were scaled to have a mean of 0 and standard deviation of 0.5. I also have an analysis in which the outcome is a 1 or 0 (i.e., correct/incorrect).

Thanks for the recommendation about the priors. I'm wondering if you'd have a general recommendation for what a reasonable scale to try would be with the variables I mentioned above?

e+42 favoured the null hypothesis.

BF with a normal (0/1) was 22.22; with a normal (0/10) was 226.11.

I'm attaching a summary output for each of the models.



Thank you very much!

messages.subject: Re: [brms-users] Reporting question
parts:
The e+42 is definitely not valid (way to large). Something went wrong in the estimation of the marginal-likelihood I suppose.

the normal(0, 1) prior (and corresponding BF) looks somewhat more reasonable, but I cannot give you a general recommendation really regarding priors for BFs. There is still so much work to in this regard particularily in multilevel models.
